passage:
Vishal: You've written "Football 5-6" on your exam timetable? Four days before thermodynamics?
Tenzin: Yes. Between the chapter on entropy and dinner. It's a block, like everything else.
Vishal: Won't you feel guilty?
Tenzin: I did last month, and I stared at the same page for an hour. Now I run, I sweat, and the page makes sense afterwards.
Vishal: Fine, I'll come. But I'm terrible.
Tenzin: Good. Then nobody's keeping score.
(An hour later, muddy and laughing.)
Vishal: You're smiling.
Tenzin: And I just remembered why my entropy answer was wrong. Same time tomorrow?

qa.q: What did Tenzin write on the exam timetable?
qa.a: Football from 5 to 6, between the chapter on entropy and dinner.

qa.q: How does Tenzin feel about the football hour, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Tenzin feels settled and happy about it. Tenzin treats it as a block like any other and is smiling afterwards.

qa.q: What choice kept the hour from turning into guilty procrastination?
qa.a: Tenzin fixed it on the timetable between chapters, so it was a planned block for recovery, and went back to the work afterwards.

qa.q: How does Vishal's view of the football hour change?
qa.a: Vishal starts out doubtful and asks about guilt, but joins in and sees Tenzin smiling and remembering the entropy answer, so the hour begins to look useful.

grounding: A stressed student schedules an hour of football and finds the mind returns sharper.

passage:
My name is Mridul, and in the week my thesis chapter was due I nearly deleted Friday's board-game night. Gopika, who lives in the next room, knocked anyway. "One hour," she said. "Bring your worst face."
I went with my head still full of footnotes. We played a silly trading game, and I lost badly and shouted at a plastic sheep. Somewhere in the second round my shoulders dropped.
The next morning the paragraph I had been circling for days took ten minutes. I used to think rest had to be earned by finishing. Now I put the games on the calendar first, like a lab slot, and defend them.

qa.q: What did Mridul nearly delete from the week?
qa.a: Friday's board-game night.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling at the start of the game night and in the second round?
qa.a: At the start Mridul was tense, with a head full of footnotes. In the second round the shoulders dropped, a sign of relaxing.

qa.q: What change in planning did Mridul make after that week?
qa.a: Mridul now puts the games on the calendar first, like a lab slot, and defends them.

qa.q: How might Gopika see Mridul's week?
qa.a: Gopika may see a stressed person who needs a break. She knocks anyway, asks for just one hour and jokes about a worst face so it is easy to say yes.

grounding: A stressed student who schedules an hour of play finds the mind returns sharper.

passage:
Hostel warden's note, Block C, Thursday night.
Zubin, second year, has been at his desk every time I pass, even at 1 am, lights on, same chapter open. Today he said he'd read one page of thermodynamics for an hour and remembered none of it. His jaw was tight.
I didn't lecture. I told him the Block C football match starts at 6 and they're one short. He said he had no time. I said, "One hour. Then you can go back."
He played. Badly, he says, laughing. He came back muddy, ate two helpings at dinner, and at 9:30 told me he'd finished the chapter and actually understood the cycles.
Plan: remind him that Thursdays are football.
Pooja

qa.q: When does the Block C football match start?
qa.a: It starts at 6, and the team was one short.

qa.q: What does Zubin's tight jaw suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he was stressed and frustrated, stuck on one page for an hour without remembering any of it.

qa.q: Why did Pooja's suggestion work?
qa.a: An hour of football gave Zubin's mind a real break; afterwards he finished the chapter and understood it.

qa.q: What would change if Pooja had told Zubin to keep studying?
qa.a: Zubin might have stayed stuck at his desk late into the night, rereading the same page without taking it in.

grounding: Shows a stressed student who plays an hour of football and returns to study with a sharper mind.

passage:
Wednesday, 11 pm
Placement tests in eight days, and I almost skipped salsa tonight. Hemant texted at 6:45, "You coming or you dying?" I said dying. He sent a sad dancing emoji, and I felt guilty enough to go.
It was ridiculous. I stepped on Hemant's feet about nine times and we spun into the wall once. I laughed so hard my stomach hurt. For one whole hour I didn't think about aptitude questions once.
Then I came home and did two practice sets in forty minutes, faster than all week. My head feels clean, like someone opened a window in there.
Note to self: salsa is part of the prep, not a break from it.
Bidisha

qa.q: About how many times did Bidisha step on Hemant's feet?
qa.a: About nine times.

qa.q: How did Bidisha feel after salsa?
qa.a: Bidisha felt lighter and clear-headed, as if a window had opened, after laughing hard enough for a stomach ache.

qa.q: What note did Bidisha write, and why is it a wise one?
qa.a: "Salsa is part of the prep, not a break from it", because the hour of play made the practice sets go faster.

qa.q: What might Hemant have been thinking when sending "You coming or you dying?"
qa.a: Hemant was probably worried Bidisha was overdoing the prep and wanted to nudge Bidisha out for a fun hour.

grounding: Shows a stressed student treating an hour of dance as part of recovery and finding the mind sharper afterwards.

passage:
Ten days before the semester exams at the agricultural college in Ludhiana district, Gurleen had stopped doing anything except study. She read the same page on soil nitrogen four times and remembered none of it. Her head felt stuffed with cotton.
Her friend Vijay found her in the hostel reading room. "You look terrible. Kabaddi on the back field at six. One hour. Come."
"I don't have time for games."
"You don't have time not to."
She went, grumbling. For an hour she ran, shouted, fell in the dust and laughed so hard at Vijay's clumsy raid that her stomach hurt.
Back in her room, showered, she opened the soil nitrogen page. This time it made sense on the first read. She finished the chapter by ten.
The next day she wrote "6 pm: kabaddi" in her timetable, in ink.

qa.q: What time did Vijay say kabaddi was?
qa.a: Vijay said kabaddi on the back field at six.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling before she went to play?
qa.a: Gurleen felt stressed and foggy, her head stuffed with cotton, and guilty about taking time off.

qa.q: What did Gurleen learn, and how did she act on it?
qa.a: She learned that an hour of play helped her mind recover, so she wrote "6 pm: kabaddi" in her timetable in ink.

qa.q: How does Vijay see play during exam time?
qa.a: Vijay sees it as necessary, not wasted, which is why he says Gurleen doesn't have time not to play.

grounding: A stressed student schedules an hour of kabaddi and finds her mind returns sharper, showing play is a recovery tool.
